That there was a puddle there at all was very strange, since it had not rained.
178485: A farmer who had come back drunk from the village sat eating in his house. At a certain moment a beige cat crept in through the water drain. When the farmer spoke to the cat, the animal replied: "Well, well, well, farmer X said to me, what a pretty beige cat you are!"
178486: Around a Templars' farmstead in Loppem there was a moat with a drawbridge. In the cellar there, sounds were heard as if bread was being baked and butter churned, although there was nothing to be seen.
178487: A farmer's wife went to confession on a Saturday evening. As she walked along the church path, she had to pass two vegetable gardens closed off by a gate. At the second gate stood a woman. During confession the farmer's wife spoke about the woman she had seen standing there. The priest then said: "On the way back you will not see that woman any more." And so it was.
178489: At the Kruisstraat between Deerlijk and Sint-Louis a calf sat every night. People believed it was a dead person who had returned. Because everyone was afraid at that crossroads, a statue of Our Lord on the cross was put up there.
178508: In Middelkerke lived a priest who competed with the doctor because he went to pray over the sick. While the priest was praying, he fixed the doctor to the ground by magic. In the end a more powerful clergyman had to be brought in to free the doctor. Priests and friars also had magic powers.
178511: A big black cat that nobody could catch always came into a house. One day the woman managed to hit the cat on the backside with a poker. When the woman went to the Oosthoek the next day, she met an old woman who was limping and who claimed she had fallen.
178514: A farmer's wife said to a woman visiting her: "People say you are a witch, but even if you bewitch everything here, I still won't believe it." The witch did not answer and went on her way. The next day, however, the farmer's wife could no longer make butter. When the cow calved, the calf looked like a monster. After the farmer's wife had been to the friars, the torments came to an end.
178528: A witch lived in Westvoorde. A woman who was praying to Our Lady was suddenly seized by the shoulders. The woman began to tremble. She was ill for a long time and the doctor could not cure her. (1) Later the witch passed her magic arts on to her daughter.
178529: In the old days it was said that the dead returned to the place where they had hidden money.
178561: The mother of a farmhand from Middelkerke could do witchcraft. For example, the witch had made a child ill with the evil hand. One day the witch made it so that a woman could no longer get home. The woman kept seeing the witch's face in front of her. After the woman had been taken home, the parish priest was sent for.
178630: In Westrozebeke lived a witch who could stop a carter travelling with his horse and cart.
178634: Someone saw a tall woman in white going into the garden at night and digging something up. The woman had to come back after her death because she had hidden something somewhere.
178660: Stalkeersen (will-o'-the-wisps) were the souls of murdered people who came back.
178670:
One Sunday evening three brave young men decided to drive away the cats at the castle of Rumbeke. Before setting off, the lads had a drink at the inn 't Lindeke by the Katteput.
When the lads were surrounded by cats, they began kicking at the animals. But they did not manage to hit a single cat and were exhausted in no time. When the lads had had enough of the game, they went home. The devil probably had a hand in it. For the next few days the three lads lay in bed with fever. Eventually the mother of one of the lads told the priest the story of the cat witches, as she called them. The clergyman replied: "On Sunday everything will come to light. After the last gospel I will leave my missal open on the altar. The witches will then be unable to leave the church."
When the priest did as he had announced the following Sunday, no fewer than fourteen women remained sitting in the church. As soon as the priest had closed the book, the witches ran out as fast as they could through the endeldeur (1).
178674:
A house in Zillewege suffered much misfortune. The clergy came to banish the ghosts to the farthest end of the land.
One evening an old woman was seen walking past. People were convinced that this woman was responsible for the misfortune they had suffered.
178732: Every day a woman came to a farm to fetch milk. When suddenly no butter could be churned on the farm anymore, a woman went to the priest. "We are not allowed to do that," the priest replied, "you must go to the friars of Tielt for that." The friars advised the farmer to put manure in the butter churn. When the woman responsible for the harm came by, they were to light the fire, so that the woman would ask to leave. When she asked for the third time, they could let her out. After they had done this, butter could be churned on the farm again.
178733: Some Belgians who had fled had caught a fine goat and put the animal in a pen. When these people were sitting outside one summer evening, a coloured toad crawled towards the goat, which began to bleat loudly. In the end the animal had to be stabbed to death.
178748: On a farm in Ledegem, the horses came outside at night without anyone having untied them. A sheep sat on the barn. After a while the horses came back sweating and all on their own. In the morning everything was normal again and the sheep on the barn had disappeared.
178751: In Adinkerke lived a little woman everyone was afraid of. During the war a sergeant asked her for lodging. "No, I don't want soldiers in the house," the woman said, and shut the door. The sergeant then said: "Fifteen soldiers are left over and they must sleep here." He wrote on the door: "Room for fifteen soldiers." It took him a good quarter of an hour to write it. When the sergeant went on, he found to his great astonishment that there was no writing on the door.
178767: When you were ridden by the maar (nightmare spirit) at night, you had a nightmare. Nightmares were caused by a person who had power over the sleeper.
178776: When someone had died in a house, people were sometimes afraid to walk past it because they believed the spirit of the dead person was still there. That fear could sometimes last for weeks.
178798: A woman from Lapscheure who had gone to steal eggs met a German shepherd on the way, who said: "You've stolen a lot of eggs, haven't you!" When the woman opened her apron, mice jumped out. The eggs fell and broke on the ground.
178818: A man walking home one evening was followed by a sheep. When the man reached his house, the sheep strangely enough became bigger than he was.
178819: At a farm there was a large gate and a small gate. Animals that were led out through the small gate had accidents. So that entrance was bricked up.
178820:
In Hooglede lived a witch who could bewitch children so that they got a heart disease. The witch always said: "Such an egg, such a child, such a tree, such a stump,...".
Some people left the witch standing at the bottom of the stairs because they were too afraid to let her in.
178821: In the past many children and adults were bewitched. People to whom this happened had to have the priest read prayers over them. Sorcerers and witches could also make it impossible for people to churn butter. Such people could bewitch someone by touching them.
178826: A rich freemason left all his possessions to public poor relief after his death. The possessions were not to be sold, because the freemason believed he would come back after his death. After his death the freemason appeared in a tree every evening to see how things were going in Ieper and to check whether the wishes in his will had been carried out.
178828: A man who was often ridden by the maar (nightmare spirit) was always thrown out of his bed.
178849: A boy had to run an errand in Lokeren. On the way back he rolled a cigarette and went into an inn for a drink. However hard he searched, he could not find his matches, although he was sure he had brought them. When the boy got home and sat down by the stove, the matches were suddenly lying on his knee.
178856: On New Year's Eve four or five people went to Bellegem to fetch a bottle of gin. Nobody dared to go alone because there was a doodkeers (death candle) somewhere along the way. On the way the company saw the doodkeers. A brave man went to the churchyard, where he saw someone standing with a sheet over his head. The man took away the sheet and to his great fright saw a ghost. When the man got back to his friends, everyone was thunderstruck. As soon as the door was shut, the ghost struck the door with his hand, and it was covered in drops of candle wax. The priest advised the brave man to go back to the churchyard the next evening at about the same time. He had to walk three times around the churchyard clockwise with the sheet in his hand. But the man went around the churchyard the other way, whereupon the ghost said: "That is not how it goes". The man put the sheet back on the ghost and ran away. Afterwards the man fell ill. A year later he died.
178867: A family in Torhout had a baby that cried all the time after it had been touched by an old woman.
178874: One morning a farmer found a bearskin in the woodpile on his farm. The farmer took the skin and threw it into the oven. The moment the skin caught fire, the farmer heard a scream and saw the farmhand throw down his tools and come inside shouting. The farmhand held his arms in the air and was foaming at the mouth with fear. "The werewolf will kill me!" he cried. The farmer replied: "You needn't be afraid, because now you are released. But during Advent you must no longer walk past Bouvelo's wood, or else the werewolf will put a new skin on you".
178878: People at sea often saw the devil standing there. But when they wanted to catch him, he was already standing somewhere else.
178885: The maar (nightmare spirit) looked like a bundle of wool that held its victim down. Anyone who wanted to protect himself against the maar had to put his slippers upside down next to his bed.
178888: A woman who was always being pestered by a man from the village sought advice from a little old woman from Brugge. The old woman told her: "Just you watch, that man won't get into your house again!" When the woman met the troublesome man three days later, he said: "Yesterday, when I reached the third tree on the road to your house, I suddenly got a stabbing pain so that I couldn't go on. That must be because of that woman you went to see?" The woman pretended not to know anything, but she knew the man was right.
178900: Whenever farmers drove their horse carts past the house of a certain woman, the carts always broke. If that woman touched the wheel of a cart, the cart ran into the horses' hindquarters.
178906: If children had a blue tree on their back after death, they had been bewitched.
178919: Doodkeersen (death candles) were dead people who came back in the form of little lights moving in the dark.
178925: Someone heard three knocks on a coffin at midnight.
178928: A man going to work greeted a passer-by on the way. That day the man could not find his house again. He wandered around for a good four or five hours.
178940: A smith was often visited by a woman who asked him foolish questions or gave him petty jobs. One day the woman gave the smith's maid a pat on the shoulder. The maid was making a chain to sell by the metre in Hazebroek. If the chain broke, it could not be sold. The woman said to the maid: "I see you haven't done it well; your chain will be returned to you. Doesn't doing all that make you ill?" The maid replied: "My work has never been returned to me." When the maid went to Hazebroek a few days later, all her work was returned. After that she lay ill in bed for two or three weeks. Moreover, the smith could no longer shoe a horse, because the animals were very restless in the smithy. After the girl had told her father everything, the father went to the friars. The clergymen advised him to put an Easter nail under the front door and under the door of the smithy. In the stall where the horses were put to be shod, a double Easter nail had to be laid. When the witch came to visit two days later, she could not get into the house or the smithy. "Well," the witch said to the smith, "are you trying to play a trick on me? I can't get in." The smith replied: "You'll be punished for what you have done to us!" For six months the witch lay paralysed in her bed. After that there were no more problems in the smithy.
178947: A man walking home along the IJzer heard sounds behind him. The faster the man walked, the faster the sounds followed one another. That was haunting.
178958: On a farm in winter people suddenly saw a strong wind rise. They saw a pig walking around and decided to put the animal in a pen. When they opened the pen the next morning, the pig had disappeared.
178993: A woman had to get up every night around twelve o'clock because she was forced to walk around the farmyard. One night her husband woke up while the woman was gone. He took his gun and shot at a dog he just saw jumping over the hedge. After that incident the woman never had to get up at night again. The next day the dog's footprints could still be seen in the potato field.
179002:
Framassons (freemasons) met in a dark place where the devil appeared and where they had to renounce their faith on the cross. Framassons had everything they wished for and they were warned when the end of their life was near.
In Avelgem there lived an unmarried pharmacist who, after the First World War, lived with a young girl. One day, when the girl was changing to go to the fair, the doorbell rang. The pharmacist saw a tall gentleman dressed in black, who had come for him. Five minutes later the gentleman was gone again. Afterwards the pharmacist told his wife that he no longer felt much like going to the fair. In the end, however, the two went anyway. When the pharmacist got into bed that night, he suddenly let out a loud cry. He was dead. The girl ran into the street in terror and went mad.
179007: One evening a man came across a rabbit. When the man wanted to strike at the rabbit, the animal jumped over the ditch. Five metres further on the rabbit was standing there again. When he got home, the man saw that the rabbit had vanished.
179008: Fishermen did not take gingerbread to sea, because they believed the trip would then be a poor one.
179010: In Koekelare a witch had driven a man to suicide. Whenever someone was pregnant, the witch always made sure she was present in that house. One day a man on a bicycle met the witch in the wood of Wijnendale. Although the witch was on foot, she arrived in Koekelare at the same time as the man. Because the curate could not absolve the witch, she had to go to the parish priest. The witch always went to confession when nobody else was in the church.
179011: A carter who was afraid of nothing said that he had sometimes had to drive through a great fire or through a thousand cats.
179075:
In Tiegem lived a woman with special powers. Every day she laid an egg in the street. After a while her son asked: "Why do you put all those eggs there?", to which the mother replied irritably: "Because I like putting them there!" Some time later all those eggs turned black.
One night the son woke up and cried: "Mother, why are you coming into my room?", to which the mother answered: "What? Am I in your room? I didn't know." That night the boy fell ill. Everyone who had been in the woman's house fell ill.
179093: A woman was assisted by her mother during childbirth. One day the newborn child began crying incessantly, so the mother had the child overlezen (read over with prayers) by the friars of Ieper. The friars said the child was being tormented by someone sticking pins. It later turned out that the child's grandmother was the culprit. After that the child no longer cried.
179097: In Passendale there lived a witch. A little cat was always walking around near her house. As soon as the cat came near the house, it suddenly disappeared. One day a white calf lay bawling against the hedge. A farmer's son took his gun and shot at the animal. The next day the witch had a wound on her buttocks.
179119: In Uitkerke stood a castle that was haunted. One day a boy from the neighbourhood said to his father: "Look, father, it's haunted there!" The father, however, saw nothing. The woman who came to haunt that castle was dressed in white when it was dark and in black when it was light.
179131: Near Zillebeke, along the road to Ieper, there were two woods that had grown together over the road. In the evening cats always sat miaowing at that spot. Passers-by were so afraid that they hardly dared to go there.
179156: Someone was always ringing the priest's doorbell and then quickly running away. "I would really like to know who that is," said the priest. When the joker came to ring the bell again, he had to stay standing there until the next morning.
179161: A man who was ridden by the maar (nightmare spirit) felt as if an animal was lying on his heart, so that he could not breathe and was completely paralysed.
179167: A lacemaker was sent by her mistress to a woman to fetch water. That woman, however, was said to be a witch. When the lacemaker came back, her mouth was where her jaw normally was. The girl looked at herself in the mirror and got a terrible fright. When the girl later kept an inn in Ieper, one could still see that her mouth was crooked.
179185: In Vinkem the witheren (white lords, ghostly white-robed monks) came to say masses.
179216: A man who was melting pig fat was annoyed by a cat that kept walking around him. The man threw the red-hot stove poker at the animal. The next day a woman from the neighbourhood had a burnt neck.
179229: A farmer who went to fetch manure suddenly saw that the chains of the cart had broken. A witch from the neighbourhood came to the farmer's aid; she lent her garter so that the horses could go on again.
179231: A woman who had gone to her sister's to fetch eggs met a witch on the way back, who said: "Have you still got them all?" The woman found she had lost some eggs and went to pick them up. Strangely enough, the fallen eggs were not broken.
179235: Since the death of the baron, the Castle of Landas in Kuurne was said to be bewitched. Every evening around midnight a horse could be seen appearing there, which had a diamond on its head and was wrapped in a hood (?). At night the clatter of the horse's shoes was heard. In the end the castle was exorcised and the cellars were bricked up.
179239: A man weaving in a house in Deerlijk always saw a little light moving back and forth by the window. The man believed the light was the soul of the house's former occupant.
179242: Two men on their way to Maria-Aalter heard cracking in the woods. They saw a dog as big as a cow. The dog went along with the men as far as the inns. At the geushoek (the unconsecrated corner) by the churchyard, suicides were buried. At that spot the dog suddenly disappeared.
179260: A sorcerer who worked for a farmer had been told to rebuild the cowshed. People laughed at the sorcerer because he could do everything. So the sorcerer put his brush into a bucket of water and said: "Off you go, little mice, run along!" The next moment the shed was full of mice.
179265: A woman standing at the gate of her house saw a man passing by, who said: "Missus, I'd like to smoke a pipe, but I have no matches." The woman let the man in and gave him matches. She explained that she had two cows but could not manage to churn butter. The man went to look at the cows, stroked them and said: "There's nothing wrong with your cows. When your husband and sons come home, scoop five buckets of muck from the slurry pit and pour them into the churn." The woman did as advised and afterwards could churn excellent butter. A little later a neighbour came calling: "Come and look! The farmer's wife is covered in muck!" That farmer's wife never visited the woman again.
179272:
A farmer from Woumen could not churn butter. People advised him to send away the first woman who came by the next morning. The first woman to come by was a woman from the village with a bad reputation.
People whose children were ill went on foot to the friars of Ieper. The friars then read prayers over the child for a good half hour.
179294: A boy from Assebroek who had accepted a coin from an old woman had nothing but bad luck.
179300: After a woman who ran a café had died, noise was always heard in the café at night; the drawers rattled and the doors opened and closed by themselves. The café owner claimed the woman came back to look for money. Masses had been promised, but the promise had not been kept. After the masses had been said, the café became quiet again.
179312:
In the old days there were many werewolves. For two months the werewolves had to go about with a skin on their backs. When the werewolf period was over, those people hid their skin in a willow or on the Kluisberg.
With that skin the werewolves could fly over the Scheldt. They had to eat everything they came across.
Every evening a werewolf prowled around the house of a girl. When the girl went for a walk with her boyfriend one day, she took a spool of yarn with her. When the boy came back the next day, the bits of yarn were still between his teeth.
179321: A man from Beveren had ten children, the youngest of whom lay in the cradle. One day an old midwife came to look after the baby. A little later the child was full of lice. When the child's father went to the friars, the clergymen advised him not to let that woman in any more.
179323: A witch sat reading a book with two candles beside her. Her daughter wanted to go out one Sunday, but her mother would not let her. The girl went anyway. When she reached the Rozebekeberg, she was forced to turn back. After that she grew completely crooked.
179346: A man out with his cart on a Saturday had to pass a witch's house. Right at that spot the cart overturned.
179370: A family employed a maid from Snaaskerke who could do magic. One day the maid turned the head of the family's baby back to front. After the maid was dismissed, nothing strange happened to those people anymore.
179386: In Nieuwpoort lived a framasson (freemason) who had signed a contract with the devil in blood. On his deathbed the man screamed for a priest. However, no one could get in because a big black man stood in front of his house blocking the entrance. Black dogs were running all over the house.
179393: In a village lived a childless farmer's wife who had lived in France for a while. People believed she was a witch. When she had gathered eggs, she threw them on the ground like potatoes without a single egg breaking.
179414: In Ardooie lived a woman who was said to be able to do magic. The woman always said: "They will never lay me out (1). I'll wash myself." One day the witch washed herself and put on a clean shirt. The next day she was dead.
179423: Two farmers were coming back at night with two carts and three horses from Brugge, where they had gone to fetch liquid manure. On the Torhoutsesteenweg near the Tillegembos, the farmers saw a procession with little lights and sound approaching. Scared to death, the farmers hid behind their cart. Later it turned out that nobody in the neighbourhood knew anything about the procession.
179428: Beets could be ridden by the maar (nightmare spirit). The plants, normally two fingers thick, then became as flat as a coin. People who were ridden by the maar had to hang a walnut branch above their bed. A man who had fallen victim to the maar had tried to catch it, but he had not succeeded.
179442: A farm in Meulebeke was haunted. One day, when the son was walking along the lane, he was slapped on the ear by an invisible figure. When the boy got home, he fell ill and even coughed up blood. Because people suspected that the place was under the influence of evil, a chapel was built on the lane. Later the little chapel was demolished because people wanted to build houses on the former lane. In one of those new houses, something was always heard knocking in the attic at midnight. After the friars had been called in, the occupants of the house decided to move. The evil must have been right on that spot, for it comes a little closer every year.
179447: Two women went to keep watch by a man who had been lying on his deathbed for several days. On the way the women met a big black dog, which suddenly vanished at the man's house. That same evening the man died.
179474: A farm in Klerken was haunted. The cows lowed restlessly and were tied by their tails to the ceiling. The dung heap was full of snakes. The friars advised the people to pour linseed on the ground. After this had been done, no more strange sounds were heard. The next day all the linseed was back in the barrel.
179477: Next to a farm was an orchard with large pear trees. Sometimes at night a woman walked among those trees with egg baskets on her arms. When people went to look, however, the woman had vanished without a trace.
179489: In Adinkerke lived a woman said to be a witch. If that woman had passed a farm in the evening, the cows there died and the children were bewitched.
179494: A woman who could do witchcraft owned books in which the magic arts were described. At dusk that woman could make everything in the house dance. When people in the street called the woman a witch, they flew to the other side of the street and fell to the ground there.
179499: A gentleman found an ugly skull with eyes like burning coals in a churchyard. The man took hold of the skull and mockingly invited it to his table. That night the doorbell rang. The frightened servant opened the door and then told the gentleman that an ugly ghost with fiery eyes was at the door, claiming to be invited. But the guests called out: "No, we are already here." Then the ghost came in and said it was the host's grandfather. The ghost seized the host, dashed his brains against the wall and dragged the damned man off to hell. The guests all dropped dead.
179528: A man and a woman went with their sick little daughter to the friars of Roeselare. The clergymen advised the parents to pray before sunrise. When the parents did so, the witch who had bewitched their child came to visit. After that the girl slowly recovered.
179537:
A fisherman who met a priest on his way to the boat on a Friday went back home and a little later set off for the boat again.
Fishermen who saw a priest standing on the quay as they sailed also believed they would have bad luck. But if they went straight to their cabin, they would still have a good voyage.
179563: In Eggewaartskapelle lived a witch who owned books of magic. If this woman drew a line on the ground, the hens could not get past it. After the witch had received a visit from a friar, she could no longer do witchcraft.
179569: A woman who worked as a maid for a gentleman had promised to build a chapel. The woman had forgotten that promise, however. The new occupants of the house always heard footsteps in the attic at night. After the people had heard that this maid had once promised something, they built a chapel. After that no strange noises were heard any more.
179573: People who had an 'animal-like' (?) child sought advice from a clergyman. The clergymen advised the people to put a wedding ring under a chair. If the sorceress came by again, she would not be able to get off that chair until she had freed the child. When the sorceress sat on the chair, she did indeed bring out a whole heap of pins.
179592: People who were ridden by the maar (nightmare spirit) at night had a standstill of the blood. You could protect yourself against the maar by putting your clogs upside down under the bed. On a farm where everyone was ridden by the maar, the devil was sitting in the attic. A priest then came and drove the devil away. A short time later, the farmer's wife died all the same.
179595: An orphan girl worked on a farm where a woman regularly came to fetch butter and eggs. One day the girl found frogs all over the milk pans in the cellar. People believed that the woman who came for the eggs and butter was responsible for the trouble. After Easter nails had been stuck under the threshold, the frogs were gone. That strange woman never came by again either.
179601: On a farm in Waardamme there was a little child who was ill. It seemed as if the child was being pricked by needles. After the child had been overlezen (read over with prayers) by the friars, it recovered. The people knew which woman was responsible for the harm.
179618: A man passing the Vier Linden with his empty cart had fallen asleep. A little later the man woke up because earth was being thrown in his face. Although the cart was empty, the horses could not move forward. The man whipped the animals until they bled, but it did not help. When the man went to stand in front of the horses, he saw a witch standing there. The man lashed at the witch with his whip, but he could not hit her. At a certain moment the witch had vanished, and the man could go on again.
179628: A mother with a small child took on a maid to help with the work. A few days after the maid started, the child cried all the time. Because the child also grew thinner and thinner, the priest's maid advised the mother to have the child sprinkled with holy water. The priest also gave the mother an Easter nail to put under the threshold. Eight days later the child was cured.
179630: Two old unmarried women fell out with two young women who lived opposite them. One night the young women found that their clothes had disappeared. After the friars of Diksmuide had come to say prayers over the young women's house, they said: "You need not be afraid, for your clothes will turn up again." The clothes were lying in the cesspit. One morning the young women saw their clothes hanging on the washing line. They dared not touch those clothes again until the friars had come to bless them. After that the old women could no longer enter the young women's house, because they could not get over the threshold.
179635: In Beselare a house stood empty. The owner himself did not dare to live in the house because it was haunted. One day a man was allowed to move into the house for a low price. One evening that man heard a rubbing sound at the front door. When he went to look, the sound could be heard at the back door, and a little later the man heard it everywhere. One evening the man went to fetch coal. Suddenly he heard a loud bang. After that, however, he never heard the bang again.
179662: When small children died of 'de oude man' (the old man, a wasting disease in children), people believed witchcraft was involved. A mother whose children had all died young took action against the witchcraft. After that no more of that woman's children died.
179666: A man coming back from the café saw a woman dressed in white standing by the mill. A moment later the apparition had vanished. The man's family claimed it was his first wife coming back. The man had been married twice.
179671: A mother of twins saw a witch approaching through the window. The woman hurried to hide the children, but she only had time to bring one of them to safety. The witch came in and tapped the other child on the head. That child died some time later.
179693: A farmer whose cows had all fallen ill sent for the vet. But nothing could help, for the cows all died. The vet advised the farmer to let him examine the cows next time before he bought them. The farmer bought new cows, but after a while they also fell ill. The vet then said to the farmer: "Doesn't a cat or a strange dog ever come here? You'd better send for a friar or a priest, because this is a difficult matter, you know!" The priest came and advised the farmer to shoot at the cat with something blessed. When the farmer had done so, the animal ran off howling towards Sint-Baafs. The next day a woman from the village turned out to have a wound in her hand. That woman did not dare go outside for three days.
179699: Two sisters lived on a farm that was haunted. One sister did not dare to go on living on her parents' farm, but the other did not mind. When the horses on that farm had to be brought to the stable, there was one horse in the meadow that was unusually big. As soon as they reached the stone gateway, the horse became as small as the other horses, so that it could walk under the gateway without any trouble.
179732: A dead man had returned because he had promised to go on a pilgrimage but had not kept that promise.
179733: The boys who had to draw lots for the army went to a woman from the village to ask which lot they should draw. The boys who had gone to ask escaped military service, but the others drew a bad lot.
179761: Doodkeersen (death candles) were damned spirits wandering at a place where a treasure or money lay hidden.
179787: At 't Vrijgeweed there was a pit into which church bells had been thrown in the time of the Sansculottes. Those bells could be heard ringing at night.
179807: People who had hidden gold somewhere had to return after their death to guard their money. If they could stab a knife into the spot where the money was hidden, they were released.
179818: A girl who went to school in Westende saw an ancient sorceress smoking a pipe from which little devils came out.
179859: Anyone who wanted to protect himself against the maar (nightmare spirit) had to put a knife in his clogs under his bed and sleep with a willow branch on his chest.
179873: Near Knesselare lived a German shepherd who went out every evening. One evening people saw the shepherd take a skin out of a tree stump. The farmer and his wife, who had a lot of bad luck on their farm, went to consult the friars, who said: "You must take that skin out of that tree and then heat the oven three times as hot as for baking bread". The skin had to be burned up before the shepherd returned; otherwise he would break all their necks. When the shepherd was working on a remote field the next morning, they did what the clergymen had advised. The skin had barely burned up when the German shepherd came running up, foaming at the mouth. The shepherd was released and no longer had to roam as a werewolf.
179885: When a German shepherd was angry with a farmer, he would conjure up a thousand rats on the farm.
179889: A man from Zedelgem and his wife had been visiting his family in Wingene. On the way back the two of them were followed the whole way by a kitten. When the man and woman reached the church, the kitten jumped into an alder hedge. A little later a calf came out of the hedge, which walked up to the woman and lifted her up.
179909: When butter could not be churned on a farm, people believed a witch had made a herbal brew.
179924: A man was married to a widow who had two sons. After the woman's death the man gave money to a little old woman to have masses said by the friars for his late wife. After a while the man's house began to be haunted. The boys were thrown up in their beds and died. The friars asked the man: "Have you ever neglected a vow? Did you actually pay for those masses for your wife?" The man answered: "Yes, I paid a little old woman for them." To that the friars said: "And did she actually hand over that money?" After it was found out that the little old woman had not handed over the money, the haunting was over.
179932: On a farm, beautiful music was always heard in the air above the bakehouse. It seemed as if a whole orchestra was playing.
179963: A man claimed that the cesspit was haunted. A sound could always be heard there. When people came closer, it went quiet.
179972: Anyone who had been frightened by something during the day could be ridden by the maar (nightmare spirit) at night. As soon as someone called out the victim's name, he was released.
179981: On a farm in Rumbeke there worked a maid who could do sorcery. In that house noise was often heard and the children were thrown up to the ceiling in their cradle. The child remained unharmed because it was given holy water every morning and evening. The beets lay scattered all over the floor. When it became known that the maid was only too eager to be rid of her sorcery, the priest was sent for to say prayers over her. That was a hard task for the clergyman. After the maid had been freed of the sorcery, she moved to America.
179990: In the old days people did not dare go to early mass alone, because between the Brakke and the level crossing a little woman haunted the road, saying: "A jug with a handle, a jug with a handle!" Someone is said to have found a great deal of money at the spot where the little woman haunted.
180004: In Gullegem lived a man who said his wife would die of lice. When the woman was dead, she was indeed full of lice.
180014: A man was lucky in the draft lottery because he had first gone to a witch, who had prayed for him. Another man also went to see the witch in the hope of being lucky too. That man, however, drew a losing lot.
180028: A lord of a castle who was out hunting had to come home because one of his parents was dying. When the hunter said he first wanted to shoot another piece of game, he was told: "Well, you may go on hunting and shooting!" Ever since, the eternal hunter could be heard calling his dog with the words: "Theo! Theo!" Around the Couthof (Proven) people are said to have heard the eternal hunter, who came back to haunt in the shape of a bird.
180035: A girl was told by a card reader that she would have to be very careful. The next day the girl fell off her bicycle. When the war broke out, the girl fell dead while standing next to her mother.
180038: A farmhand who worked in Poperinge went to his home in Vlamertinge every Sunday. Because the neighbourhood where he lived was bewitched, the boy played his accordion in the dark in the evening. One evening the boy suddenly saw a big black dog standing in front of him. When he went on, a small white dog ran in front of his feet. The boy tried to chase the dogs away, but both animals sat up on their hind legs in front of him. Terrified, the boy ran away.
180044: At a factory in Anzegem a fearless woodcutter saw more than a hundred and fifty cats jumping back and forth. When the man came closer, the cats had suddenly all vanished. A little later the cats were there again. The man came home drenched in sweat from fear.
180065: One Saturday morning a woman went to cut grass for her animals. Suddenly she saw a man in beige clothes walking across the moat bank with his head hanging. While she was cutting grass, she heard little voices. When she went home, she decided to go and look at the bridge by the moat. When she reached the moat, she got a great fright, for she found there was no bridge at all. Yet earlier that day she had seen a man walking on the bank. When she got home she told everything to her neighbour, who said: "That must have been your first husband, come to ask forgiveness." The woman's first husband had been a drunkard who often got into fights.
180067: In a house in Zwevezele the doors rattled and the bed turned at night. The farmer had been unfaithful with a woman who could do sorcery. Because the farmer no longer went to that woman, she bewitched the farm at night. The friars came to say prayers over the farm and advised the farmer to go and pray in church for three consecutive days with his arms outstretched. Because that man had never gone to church before, the villagers laughed at these practices.
180085: One evening a boy saw two spotted cows come out of a ditch. The boy ran away in fear, losing his bag and his shoes. At home the boy said he had been chased by two cows. When the boy went to look the next morning, there was no trace of the cows.
180088: When a farmer was working in his field with a roller, a witch came by and made the roller split.
180092: In Poperinge there lived a woman who seized every chance to touch a child. If she had laid her hand on a child's head, the child fell ill shortly afterwards. Bewitched children had to be taken to the friars.
180097: In a room where someone had just died, a man dressed in black appeared whom no one had ever seen before. The man picked up the body and vanished. People believed that this man was the devil.
180113: One of the returning dead disappeared after five Our Fathers had been prayed.
180133: Anyone who was ridden by the maar (nightmare spirit) had a standstill of the blood. Victims of the maar lay thrashing about in their beds.
180151: A woman was convinced that two of her children had died because of a sorceress. While the woman had gone to fetch water at the well, the sorceress was said to have come near the cradle. The woman's husband claimed that this was impossible because there were no footprints to be seen.
180168:
When a house was on fire, clergymen could put out the flames by stretching out their hand.
A young man had arranged with his fiancée to go to the priest on Friday. But the young man did not keep his promise and rode to his work in Oostende. When the girl saw her beloved ride past, she was so distressed that she jumped into the water. The girl was rescued by two people. The priest came to give her the Last Sacraments and said: "Before evening your beloved will be standing at your bed." As soon as the young man heard what had happened, he dropped his work and hurried to his beloved. That same priest had once fixed the two lovers to their church chairs by magic because they were talking during mass.
The clergyman had once said to a courting couple: "You are standing too close to my door. Go and stand somewhere else!" The young man and the girl had laughed at the clergyman's words. But on Monday morning they were still standing there! They could only move on when the clergyman had given them permission.
180177: Duitse schapers (German shepherds, travelling shepherds said to have magic powers) could tap beer from their walking sticks.
180180: People who had sold their soul to the devil at a crossroads received from the devil a little bag with a galgenjong (a devil's familiar, literally 'gallows child') in it. With it those people could do whatever they wanted. Because those people were damned, they tried everything to pass the galgenjong on to someone else. People who had made a pact with the devil could easily be recognised by the priest during Mass. When the Gospel was read, such people stood with their backs to the altar.
180195: A man who had hidden his money at the foot of a pear tree had died without being able to tell anyone where his money was. One night it looked as if the farm where the man had lived was on fire. The fire raged most fiercely at the pear tree. Some neighbours were so frightened that they decided to move away. After a long time a priest told the people: "If something like that happens again, you must say: 'Speak!'" When the people did so, a voice answered: "Dig at the foot of the pear tree on the right side of the garden. Money is hidden there!" At that spot the people did indeed find a chest of money.
180252:
In Beselare there lived an old lacemaker who went to the café every day when she had sold her lace. So that woman spent all her money on drink. In one house there was a boy of five or six who was gravely ill. When the child was taken to the friars, the clergymen said: "Is there a woman who regularly comes to your house and lays her hand on the child? You must no longer let that woman in and you must give the boy a drop of holy water every day." The people thought hard and concluded that the lacemaker might well be the woman the friar had spoken of. The lacemaker was no longer let in and the child recovered.
One day the lacemaker was visiting people from Beselare. She was already dead drunk when she arrived and asked for more beer. When the woman went to the toilet, she fell on the floor there, so that the door, which opened inwards, could no longer be opened. When the woman had finally been freed from her awkward position, it was seen that the hem of her skirt was full of papers. The woman always claimed that she could do a lot of harm with those papers.
180253: A fisherman had mocked a priest. The clergyman then said that on his way home the man would get no further than a certain spot in the dunes. When the fisherman went home, he indeed got no further than that spot.
180256: People who always heard strange knocking in their house were advised by someone to hang a white cloth outside. A while later a black hand had been burnt into the cloth. It was a soul that had come to haunt. After the people had prayed a great deal, they heard no more knocking in their house.
180283: Close to a two-family house near the mill of Beselare stood an oak tree that was bewitched. Nobody dared to walk past it. During the Second World War a Belgian soldier was found dead by that tree. Nobody in the neighbourhood had heard a shot or a scream.
180309: A broom maker drove around with his cart, pulled by a big dog. When the man came to a bridge, he kicked at a little dog that blocked his way. Further on the man saw that the little dog was following him and moreover kept getting bigger. When the man passed a crossroads, the phantom dog could go no further. Later the man told his story to a priest, who said: "If you had walked around seven or eight minutes longer, the animal would have broken your neck!" Since the Gospel of Saint John has been read after Mass, there is not so much haunting any more.
180322: A road worker's house was haunted. One day when the man came home, he found that all the paintings were hanging upside down on the wall. The man complained to his sister, who had come to clean the house. On his way home the man was followed by a big dog. When the man lay in bed, he felt someone shaking his bed, and his clogs were knocked together. One evening the brewer and the smith went to drink a glass of beer in the haunted house. Since then nothing strange has ever happened in that house again.
180334: In a small house in Abele there lived a woman who could make people fall to the ground. One evening, as the woman stood at her door, she greeted a passer-by. A little further on, that man was thrown to the ground.
180358: In the little chapel near café 't Schipleed stood a statue of Mary that was visited by pilgrims every year. Because the statue was no longer beautiful, the priest one day replaced it with a new one. That night the old statue made its own way from the sacristy through the mud to the little chapel where it had always stood.
180367: In a house where a child was ill, the occupants always heard noises in the attic as if a load of cobblestones was being thrown down. The doors flew open, although nothing could be seen. When the friars of Tielt came to say prayers over the child, they said: "There is evil at work. The culprit is a woman who comes here every day to peel. I will put something blessed under the door." After the clergyman had done that, the woman never visited again. That woman had already bewitched several children. Moreover, she was the farmer's wife's sister-in-law!
180374: People came from Knesselare, Oedelem and Eentveld to look at a stalkaars (will-o'-the-wisp) at 't Maandagsche (?). People believed the light was a returned dead person. It was probably just some joke.
180389: Sorceresses stabbed girls and women to death with pins. The more pins the sorceresses used, the faster the victims died. If the friars could overlezen (read over with prayers) the victims in time and pull the pins out of the cushions, they could sometimes still save them.
180394: On a farm in Gijzelbrechtegem they were struggling with a plague of rats, so that the laundry and even the cows were full of rats. A witch had caused it.
180407: A man on his way to his sweetheart saw a woman in silk clothing walking beside him at the Kruiskassei. The man greeted the woman, but there was no answer. At that the man ran all the way to the Schare.
180418: A woman who wanted to bake cakes found that the dough would not rise. A cat was sitting under the stove. In a fit of rage the woman threw the kettle of dough over the cat. The next day a woman from the village lay in her bed with burns.
180429: Two lovers walking past a park in Oostende one evening saw a white figure appear. The girl had always been taught by her mother that on seeing a ghost she should hold both hands out in front of her with her thumbs tucked into her fists. When the girl did so, the ghost vanished at once.
180431: The maar (nightmare spirit) was a tormenting spirit that crawled onto people and tried to strangle them.
180435:
One was not supposed to kick at a spotted cat. If one stepped over the animal, one would be in no danger.
A farmer going to early Mass on Sunday was hindered on the way by a cat. The farmer kicked at the animal, but lost his shoe doing so. The farmer never found that shoe again. He had also been injured in the leg.
180445: Sorcerers owned a book with which they could cause a plague of rats. When that happened, rats ran everywhere in a house or on a farm and destroyed everything, except statues of Christ and Mary.
180451: Some children from Markesteert had fallen ill after eating a pear they had been given by a woman from Moeskroen.
180460: When people had no more coal in winter, a witch would go and ask for fire somewhere in a sock. Strangely enough, the sock did not burn. The witch was burned at a crossroads in Nieuwpoort.
180466: The dead had to return to bring up hidden money or gold. Sometimes they also had to come back to answer for a sin, such as a theft in the church.
180485: In Beselare lived a man who had special powers. One Sunday at the church door the man fixed six witches wearing aprons to the ground by magic.
180493: When you were ridden by the maar (nightmare spirit), you wanted to call out, but you could not make a sound. In fact it was a standstill of the blood. If you put your shoes with the toes under the bed, you were protected against the maar.
180496: On a farm in Kaaskerke the cows were untied at night, although the animals had been tied up securely. The priest of Kortrijk came to say prayers over the stables until he was drenched in sweat. It is even said that the priest was left with an illness from it. After the clergyman had tied the cows up again, there were no more problems.
180506: A woman was compelled always to go to small children. Children whom the woman had been near did nothing but cry afterwards.
180514: A farmhand walking home in the evening was often followed by a white cat that jumped on his back.
180520: A man had told someone that he had few rats on his farm. But when the man came home, his attic was swarming with rats. To undo the spell, the man went to consult the curate.
180526: A man woke up at around three in the morning. Next to him slept a little man who asked for a bucket of water. The man answered: "Wait until it gets light." The next moment someone knocked on the window. The man felt as if a sack of grain was lying on him and he could not call his father. When the man had called out: "Our Lady, deliver me!", the weight was gone.
180540: In a family in Wingene the mother had died. The little child saw the ghost of her dead mother before her eyes all the time. One day the child said: "Father, may I have a little cross? Mother is there again and she's asking if I'll go with her." The next day the child lay dead.
180559: At the 'torrelen' the buckets of milk danced through the gate towards the street.
180567: On a farm in Ruddervoorde so much noise was heard at night that it sounded as if someone were threshing. When people got up at night to go and look, suddenly nothing could be heard. Then the noise started again. Sometimes chains could also be heard rattling at night.
180587: A poacher went hunting with a friend near the castle of Rumbeke. Although the two men had taken different paths, they saw at the same moment a hare that seemed to be invulnerable. When the men tried to shoot at the animal, their guns did not work and suddenly there were two or three hares.
180589: People who were ridden by the maar (nightmare spirit) could not sleep at night. They got up and walked around until they collapsed. Victims of the maar could have the priests read prayers over them.
180591: At night a woman saw through her window a coach carrying the dead furniture maker of Markegem floating through the air. This went on for fourteen days. Everyone went to stand outside their doors to see it.
180594: Every evening a man saw a little light hovering beside an alder hedge. One evening the man lay down beside the hedge and pretended to be dead. The light began to tickle him and then took a steam boiler full of money out of the ground. The man watched the light begin to count the money. The man released the light.
180616: Children who had been bewitched by an old woman could not walk until they were three or four years old.
180619: A man went for a walk with two priests. The three of them walked past a farm where the dog was barking loudly. The priests asked why the dog was making such a racket, and the man replied: "Don't you know? Tonight someone will break in here." On the priests' advice, the man went to warn the farmer of the trouble. The farmer asked the man for help, and the man said: "I need a one-year-old shoot from a walnut tree. Also give me twelve chairs and twelve bundles of wood." The farmer gave the man everything he had asked for. That night twelve robbers came in. "Sit down," said the man, and then he lit the fire. The robbers could no longer get up from their chairs, and they were nearly burned. After that ordeal the robbers left and never returned to that farm.
180640: Anyone who was ridden by the maar (nightmare spirit) felt hair everywhere and felt as if his throat was being squeezed shut. To protect yourself against the maar, you had to put your clogs upside down under the bed and sleep with your arms crossed. Some people claimed that the maar was a standstill of the blood.
180669: At the Rattekot in Watou they were struggling with a real plague of rats. Someone had sent those rats to the house.
180675: In his house in the Groenstraat a man was chased by one of the returning dead, who had taken a chisel from the workbench and threw it at him. He (the man or the ghost?) walked on the roof while complaining that he (?) was not master.
180685: Around midnight at the Hulhoek two men saw a goat dancing and leaping about. The lads tried to catch the goat, but did not succeed. At the crossroads the goat had suddenly vanished.
180690: A witch turned herself into a cat and in that shape went scratching at people's houses.
180718: At the fair in Assebroek a pregnant woman had shaken hands with a witch. Later that woman's child got 'de oude man' (the old man, a wasting disease in children). The woman then had to go begging to be able to have a mass said for her child. In the end the child did recover.
180725: The maar (nightmare spirit) is a standstill of the blood, which gave you itching or pain at night.
180730: A dead farmer who had to come back walked around all night with a bluestone post on his shoulder. The farmer had once moved a boundary post of his field. After someone said to the farmer: "Put it back where you got it", the ghost no longer appeared.
180733: A German shepherd flew to Germany every Saturday to fetch a clean shirt. One day a farmhand decided to fly along with the German shepherd. On the way the pair heard a bang. It was the horse's hoof striking the tower of the Church of Our Lady.
180739: A farmer went to fetch the doctor for his wife, who was about to give birth. When the farmer saw a horse-drawn cart approaching, he thought it was the doctor. A moment later, however, the cart had vanished without a trace.
180745: A man walking past the 'spokkelboske' was thrown to the ground by a strange force at the same spot every time. As soon as the man had scrambled to his feet, he received another blow, which made him fall again.
180761: A man taking eel to 't Nieuwland met a woman on the way. Shortly afterwards the man was lying in the brook.
180788: A pregnant woman who was taking butter to the market in Kortrijk met a little old woman on the way, who came to sit beside her and talked to her. That day the pregnant woman went home terrified. Her child was never normal. One day, when the woman's children were playing, that one child stood looking at the door. For there stood the witch who had bewitched the child.
180794: A plant grower saw a hare running among the tobacco plants and went home to fetch a gun. When the man came back, he saw a woman walking. Perhaps that woman had changed into the hare a few moments earlier. A witch animal could only be shot if one had put something blessed in one's gun.
180804: In Harelbeke lived a sorceress who got up at midnight and sat in her armchair wearing a beautiful cloak. That sorceress had a cupboard holding little wax dolls. If she wanted to bewitch someone in the parish, she went to one of those dolls.
180827: In Blankenberge there lived an old woman who was suspected of being a witch. One day a mother with a newborn baby came to visit the old woman. The woman took the baby in her arms and said: "What a beautiful baby!" Two days later the baby was dead.
180865: A newly married man could not sleep well. He had been in bed less than five minutes before he could no longer speak and began moving his hands and feet. His worried wife ran in her nightgown to the man's parents, who lived in the house across the street. The parents advised the woman to say the man's name. When the woman did so, the man was released at once. They had already tried all sorts of things, for example sleeping with a bread knife or with a straw on his chest, but nothing had helped. The parish priest had also come by. In the end, saying the name turned out to be the best remedy.
180877: A man who was often out in the evening was always followed by a dog at a farm. When the man turned around to hit the animal, he found to his great fright that a big man was standing behind him.
180886: In the Nachtegaleweide between Vladslo and Leke people saw a headless horse every night. Later a cross was put up in that meadow.
180915: A man claimed he saw his dead mother return in the attic every night. So the man built a little chapel.
180930: There was a large linden tree on a farm. If someone passed by there around ten or half past ten, it was haunted. That is why a chapel was built near that tree.
180932: A witch conjured a farm full of white hens. At noon five tomcats were eating the porridge, although no tomcats had been seen there before.
180943: A parish priest met a robber, who asked him for his gold watch. "Wait, I'll go and fetch my watch," said the priest, and he bewitched the robber so that he was fixed to the ground. A little later the robber's wife came past that spot. Astonished, she said to her husband: "But what are you doing here?" The next moment the robber could move on again.
180966: On a farm where butter could no longer be churned, the friars of Moerkerke were sent for. The friars walked around the farm praying and blessed the building. After that the farm never again had problems with churning.
180981: After a witch had visited a farm, the farmer could no longer churn butter.
181007: Maretakken (mistletoe, literally mare branches) were branches that had been ridden by the maar (nightmare spirit). A man who was always ridden by the maar at night hung some mistletoe above his bed. That helped the man.
181010: A farmer's wife could not churn butter because a strange woman was always visiting her. That woman was a witch. After the farmer's wife had been to the curate, she could churn butter again.
181039: In a family where the mother had died, the eldest daughter saw her mother's ghost appear two or three times a week. The ghost always appeared by the pump and then went to stand in front of the daughter's bed. The dead mother shone like a star.
181063: A farm was haunted. At night people heard beautiful music and footsteps in the attic, but when they went to look, there was nothing to be seen.
181072: A beachcomber met the priest, who said indignantly: "Well, are you going to the beach again on a Sunday?" On the beach the beachcomber found a small wooden stick. The following night at twelve o'clock the beachcomber was standing on a high dune with the stick.
181076: At night a man heard carts driving across the yard, although there was nothing to be seen.
181093: On a farm in Geluveld butter could no longer be churned. After a friar from Ieper had come to say prayers over the farm, butter could be made again.
181100: A man could not manage to haul trees with three horses. A little later a farmer came by and said: "I have bewitched the horses so they are fixed to the ground." When the sorcerer had harnessed his own horse to the cart, the cart moved off effortlessly.
181104: An altar boy was standing in the pulpit imitating the parish priest. At that very moment a big dog with a cross on its tail came into the church. It was believed that the dog was a witch who had turned herself into an animal.
181120:
Every night the hell wagon drove around with farmhands who had written their names in blood in a big book. Those farmhands had been given a bearskin with which they had to go haunting.
On a farm where there was much bad luck, the farmer sent his farmhand to Holland on some job or other. When the farmhand had been gone for a while, the farmer heated the oven to burn the farmhand's bearskin in it. The skin had barely caught fire when the farmhand came flying home like a bloodhound through hedges and bushes. When he got home, however, the farmhand found that the bearskin had already burned up completely. The farmhand thanked the farmer on his knees for releasing him.
181134: A woman came to visit a house where a child was ill. The child's father grew angry and demanded that the woman stop tormenting his child. For the woman had a little doll into which she stuck pins.
181136: A man coming back from Roesbrugge did not reach his home until around ten in the morning. The man was drenched in sweat because he had been ridden by the maar (nightmare spirit).
181154: Every night there were little lights around the farm near the Hoogmolen. They were returned dead. When a fearless man went to look, all the lights flew down. The man was thrown into the ditch by one of the lights and pulled by his hair.
181156: People who were ridden by the maar (nightmare spirit) hung mistletoe above their bed. The maar then sat on the branch instead of on its victim.
181168: Some woodcutters walked home together after work. One of the men was in the habit of poaching and said: "Last night I saw a burning candle standing here on this log." The men went to the café together. At night the poacher went back to the woods to pull the log out of the ground. The next day he no longer went along with the other woodcutters and said: "I'm not working any more, I want to live a bit more quietly." The other men were convinced their companion had dug up a treasure.
181183: A horse groom walked home one evening to the Brantoek. Because he was afraid, he took an accordion along. On the way he met a big and a small dog. When the little dog knelt, the groom was so frightened that he ran home as fast as he could.
181192: A miserly baron lived in Merkem. When the baron had died, someone from Merkem had said that his death was not so bad, because the man had never done anything for anyone else anyway. The baroness had heard what people were saying and sent her servant to the village. Every evening the villagers heard the call of a strange bird in the woods. People believed it was the ghost of the baron, who had to come and atone for his miserliness. When the baroness heard this too, she sent her servant to the village with a dead owl. The servant had to visit everyone and say that the baron was not haunting, because the strange bird had now been caught. That same evening, however, the villagers heard the bird's call again and said: "You see, it is the baron after all!"
181211: Between sleeping and waking you could be ridden by the maar (nightmare spirit). When that happened, you could not move because you were pressed down by a strange force.
181219: In Leke lived many women who could bewitch children. One day a woman came to visit a child who cried all the time. The woman then said: "I can well believe that child always cries! It is lying on pins!" Only that woman could see the pins. Most likely it was she who had bewitched the child.
181227: A woman who was boiling potatoes saw a kitten approaching and poured the boiling potatoes over the animal. When the woman got up the next day, she saw her neighbour lying on the floor, burned all over. Because the neighbour was a sorceress who had already done much harm, she was punished and had to turn herself into a cat.
181237: A carter always saw a white lady wearing silk clothing appear in the beech lane. One day his neighbours advised the man to speak to the lady. The next evening the carter stopped by the apparition and said: "If you are sent by God, speak. If you are sent by the devil, vanish". The words had barely left his mouth when he received a blow that knocked him to the ground.
181243: At a little house where a wizard lived, a big black dog was seen sitting at the window every evening, although people knew the wizard had no dog. The dog was the wizard himself.
181244: On a farm in Rollegem-Kapelle a dead woman came to haunt at midnight, saying: "Half milk, half water, alas my soul." During her life the farmer's wife had always poured water into the milk she sold.
181266: A dead man came back because he had forgotten his purse, his pipe and his tobacco.
181268: An old lame woman had a child that was bewitched. The child could not walk and was not toilet-trained. That woman's three other children were simple-minded. The woman went to mass every day.
181303: Some girls on their way to the fair walked past a farm where a German shepherd was sitting in the grass. The girls did not greet the shepherd. A little later, however, they found that they were full of lice and fleas, so that they had to turn back. When the shepherd saw the girls pass by again, he said: "That will teach you! Next time you won't mock people any more!"
181319: Four people, among them a strange little woman, were playing cards. The little woman always had the four jokers. Because another player laughed about it, the little woman said: "Just wait, next time you will have them!" And so it was.
181322: In a house in Ardooie all the children fell ill. The priest came to read prayers over the children, but they died. People believed the misfortune was caused by a cat that always came in through the drain hole for the water. One day the cat was beaten to death. The next day it was found that the neighbour had died.
181355: A man was always accompanied on his way home by a dog a metre tall. The man looked the animal straight in the eyes, but afterwards he never dared to take that same road again.
181360: Two men were coming back from an inn at night. Suddenly one of them said: "Whatever appears, I want to ride on it. Even if it were a donkey, I want to ride on it". The words were barely out of his mouth when a donkey appeared. But the man was too afraid to ride the donkey. The faster the men walked home, the faster the donkey followed them.
181404: A man went with his sisters to Gotelartjes to sell lace there. When on the way back the man passed the castle of Vonderbeke, he saw a whole row of tall trees there in which cats were playing. The man was not afraid, but his sisters were.
181405: In Kaster there was a pit where strange things happened. When people walked past the pit, it suddenly grew very windy and a strange whooshing was heard. When the trees around the pit were removed, leather money was found there. After it had been taken to the priest to have masses said, nothing strange happened at the pit any more. It had been a dead person who had returned.
181413: When a witch had died, no one could get the cart with her body to move. When the cart finally did start moving, it ran into a dike.
181414: A woman who wanted to bake bread could not put the bread in the oven because a witch had filled the oven with cobwebs by magic.
181431:
A parish priest could bewitch people who had chattered too much during mass so that they were stuck to their chairs, where everyone could see them.
If a woman had run away from her husband, the priest could make her come back.
Anyone who had lost something had to tell the priest. The clergyman could then make sure that the thieves gladly brought back the stolen goods, provided they had not yet passed into other hands.
181432: In Hooglede there lived a woman who could turn herself into a crow. She could also climb into a tree and make the sound of a crow. A tramp who passed by went into that woman's house to steal money. Police officers arrested the man and made him promise never to do such a thing again. Once, in a single night, the woman had mown a gemet (1) (an old land measure) of oats. She could also bewitch children in the cradle and make them die.
181457: A woman who was ridden by the maar (nightmare spirit) tried to call out, but no sound came.
181464: At night a man saw three women walking on crutches, followed by a man on horseback. Then the man saw a skull in front of him, which disappeared again a moment later.
181477: A small woman was married to a hunchbacked bricklayer. The woman repaired watches and was feared by people because everyone believed she could do sorcery. In the past the witch was said to have squeezed babies to death. Later a small chapel was built in front of her house to protect people against her magic power.
181481: In the past a woman who practised black magic lived in Marke. That woman had a large black bird in a cage. It was perhaps a crow. She also had several black cats. That woman could make people fall ill or get lice. Nobody dared to walk past her house. When the woman lay on her deathbed, her books were taken from her.
181489: A witch made the boys run around the church until they fell.
181516: The wife of an Iceland fisherman was always alone when she had to give birth. Then, without anyone having opened the door, the priest would come in and stand by the bed to tell the woman how her husband and her son were faring at sea at that moment. Each time the child died or was abnormal because it had been frightened. One day one of the neighbours stayed with the pregnant woman. After that the priest no longer came.
181519: A man who had been out could not get home because he was ridden by the maar (nightmare spirit). The man was forced to keep walking along the ramparts. Only when he came to a moat did he find his way again.
181527: Duitse schapers (German shepherds, travelling shepherds said to have magic powers) could drink wine from their 'makke' (1).
181534: A man whose child had just died showed a visitor the child's little back. On the back was a tree from the head to the feet. According to the child's father, a witch had done it.
181539: In Izegem lived a little old woman whom everyone feared. One day, when that woman had been with a baby, the cradle was soon full of lice. People could keep such witches from coming in by putting something blessed under the threshold and by not speaking to the witch.
181559: A man who was ridden by the maar (nightmare spirit) felt the maar crawl up his legs. If you could then no longer turn onto your side, you had to wait until the maar left of its own accord. The maar lay down on the belly of its victims.
181575: Around 1911 the hemelgeit (sky goat, a snipe-like spirit) often roamed the marshy meadows of Merkem. Every evening people went to listen on the bank of the Ijzer, where they heard a goat bleating. They believed that goat was the ghost of a dead man. For a month, three or four hundred people came every evening to listen to the bleating. Nobody dared to cross the Ijzer.
181583: In Ruddervoorde there was a pit into which 'kastanjepersen' (?) had been thrown to soak. Strange sounds were heard in that pit, such as the rattling of chains. Those sounds, however, were probably caused by the neighbours' dog.
181612: A pregnant woman had a quarrel with a witch. At a certain moment the witch struck the woman and said: "You will regret that!" Some time later the woman gave birth to a child with a deformity in the loins.
181628: In Aartrijke there lived a woman who was never allowed near small children, because people knew that woman could bewitch children.
181631: The procession of Sint-Jan was cancelled because of the bad weather. When people went to church the next day, they saw that the bottom of the statue of Mary was covered in mud. Mary had gone outside herself.
181641: An Iceland fisherman who had just returned from a voyage went to the fair. An entry ticket for the dance hall cost twenty-five centimes, but one could then go in and out all evening. The woman who checked the tickets had a crooked mouth. When the woman claimed that the Iceland fisherman had not yet paid, the man began to mock her. But he had barely entered the dance hall when his mouth was crooked too. A few days later the man even died.
181654: At the Sijseleveld at Spermalie, the nuns who had once lived there came back to haunt at night. They made noise and walked up and down the stairs.
181661: Doodkeersen (death candles) were dead people who came back because they still had something to make right.
181662: On a farm in Dadizele there were two cows, which one day stopped giving milk because the stables were bewitched. After the friars had been consulted, everything returned to normal on the farm. The place had been bewitched by a woman who lived nearby.
181669: A mother who had a small child was visited by a sorceress who took hold of the child and said: "But what a good child you have!" Shortly afterwards the child began to cry. The child's body was stuck full of pins.
181694: A man who had to transport eel at night met a flock of little swans, which said: "The day is for you, the night is for us".
181715: A little white dog always ran around in the wood. When the trees were cut down, a pot full of money was found under the roots of a large tree. After that money was found, the little dog was never seen again.
181716: At school a boy could make rats and mice run over the benches to frighten the other pupils. When the children told the teacher, he sent the little boy who could do magic home. After all, the boy was wiser than the teacher.
181717: A man got lost because of a wizard. He had to walk around for a good three hours before he could find his bearings again.
181738: A man from Middelkerke had a maid who did strange things. Every time the maid hung the steam kettle over the fire, the kettle disappeared up the chimney into the dunes. Nobody could find the kettle again except the maid herself. On the priest's advice the farmer sent his maid away.
181756: A little child who had the distel (?) in her hair went to the market with her mother. From a market stallholder the mother bought her daughter a little cap against the distel. As soon as the mother had put the cap on her child, the girl began to cry and thrash about like a cat. When the mother lifted the child, it weighed a good thirty kilos, though it was only one year old. When they got home, the father advised throwing the cap into the fire. But the cap did not burn. Only when holy water and salt had been thrown on it did the cloth catch fire. After that the child stopped crying. The priest was sent for to read prayers over the child. But the clergyman could not get inside and had to stand on the threshold for half an hour. When he finally did get in, he gave a medal to the child and to the mother. Nothing like it ever happened again. The cap seller could not get into the house.
181771: A woman had stroked the head of a small child. Afterwards the little head was full of pins. When an Easter nail had been put under the door, that woman could no longer come in.
181776: Death candles were little lights that crept over the ground. People who had seen a death candle believed that someone would soon die.
181782: In Roesbrugge lived a woman who was said to be a witch. Because butter could no longer be made on a farm and two pigs and a cow had died, the farmer's wife went to the friars. The clergymen gave her blessed salt and medals to put under the door. After that the suspected woman never came to the farm again. "It is too dirty at your place," she claimed.
181794: On a farm in Maldegem the pigs grew thin after a woman had come to look at the animals. People believed that this woman had bewitched the pigs.
181796: One evening people heard a returned dead person cry out: "Help me, help me! I am so hungry! I am suffering so terribly here, pray for me!" When the people asked what the ghost wanted, it answered: "You must give two avotten (a measure of grain) of corn to x, because I owe him that." Two days after the people had done so, the ghost appeared again, saying: "I still have so much to suffer, you must give four more avotten of corn to the same person." A few days later the people had to give ten more avotten, and some time after that they had to give twenty. When a brave man found the courage to go outside, someone ran away. The ghost was quickly released!
181807: People who took an afternoon nap were often troubled by the maar (nightmare spirit). To protect yourself against the maar, you had to put your clogs upside down next to the bed. The maar could only be caught with crossed arms. In the past there were also many mothers-in-law who stuck Easter nails at the foot of the cradle to protect the children against the maar.
181818: People who were ridden by the maar (nightmare spirit) felt as if someone was squeezing their throat shut and could no longer breathe. Victims of the maar tried to call out, but could not. You could drive the maar away by making the sign of the cross.
181827: A man going through the woods to Beselare around midnight heard the flying goat scream. Many people came to see this apparition. In reality it was a bird that bleated like a goat. One day the man's brother managed to shoot the bird down.
181850: On a farm a lid was heard slamming shut at night, along with the rattling of buckets of water. Strangely enough, there was nothing to be seen. A wall clock that had not worked for years suddenly began to strike twelve. The calves born on that farm died immediately. In the end the friars put medals between the stones in the cowshed. After that the haunting came to an end.
181855: A farmer and his wife were getting ready to leave for a funeral when a beggar came asking for a sandwich. When the farmer gave the man a slice of bread, the beggar touched his hand, thanked him and disappeared. Afterwards the farmer and his wife, and the whole house too, were full of lice. The farmer's wife went to fetch the parish priest, who came to bless the house and said prayers. In that way the priest managed to make all the lice disappear. Some time later the farmer went on an errand at the Zwarte Molen in Kemmel. When he met that beggar there, the beggar said to him: "I really had you there, didn't I!" That beggar was a German shepherd.
181860: Whoever let a black cat in at night would have bad luck.
